Polymyalgia Rheumatica

aching with normal strength · sedimentation rate and creatine kinase · giant cell arteritis overlap · prednisone responseIs this pain and stiffness with normal strength after 50, and does low-dose prednisone clear it within days?

1Script2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Illness script
Bottom line
  • Over 50, bilateral shoulder and hip girdle aching with morning stiffness, normal strength, a high erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and a normal creatine kinase (CK) polymyalgia rheumatica
  • Low-dose prednisone, about 15 mg; a dramatic response within days supports the diagnosis, and no response means another diagnosis
  • Headache, jaw claudication or vision change is giant cell arteritis: high-dose glucocorticoids now, the biopsy after
What it is

An inflammatory syndrome of proximal aching and stiffness in adults over 50, without true weakness, closely tied to giant cell arteritis

Driver

Likely low-grade synovitis and bursitis around the girdles, not muscle injury, so the CK stays normal

Triggers

Age over 50 (non-modifiable)

Female sex, about 2 to 1 (non-modifiable)

Chain

Inflammation: girdle bursitis and synovitis ESR and C-reactive protein (CRP) rise

Clinical: shoulder and hip girdle aching morning stiffness over an hour pain limits movement while strength stays normal

Insights

Pain, not weakness, keeps the patient in bed: true weakness with a high CK means myositis

The steroid response is part of the diagnosis: relief comes in hours to days on low-dose prednisone, and no response by a week points elsewhere

2Urgent risks
Giant cell arteritisNew headache, jaw claudication, vision loss or amaurosis fugax; coexists with polymyalgia rheumatica in about half

If it is suspected, choose high-dose glucocorticoids at once, IV pulse first if vision is impaired; the temporal artery biopsy follows. Temporal artery biopsyThe arteritis is segmental, so the biopsy takes a long segment, and a negative biopsy does not exclude it. Treatment is not delayed for it: the biopsy can be done up to 2 weeks after glucocorticoids start. Jaw claudication and diplopia carry a higher risk of blindness.

BlindnessUntreated arteritis blinds; jaw claudication and diplopia raise the risk

If vision is threatened, choose do not wait for the biopsy.

3Differential
Proximal pain or weakness after 50, most tempting first
DiagnosisFingerprintDecides it
Polymyalgia rheumaticaBilateral shoulder and hip girdle aching and stiffness; strength normalSudden onset; stiffness over an hour each morning; ESR and CRP high, CK normal
Polymyositis or dermatomyositisProximal weakness more than pain; dermatomyositis adds a heliotrope rash and Gottron papules and can signal a cancerCK high; anti-Jo-1; muscle biopsy confirms
Giant cell arteritis (temporal arteritis)Headache, jaw claudication, vision lossOver 50; ESR often over 50; temporal artery biopsy shows giant cells
Elderly-onset rheumatoid arthritisSmall-joint synovitis of the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) and proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints, erosionsRheumatoid factor or anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) positive
Statin myopathy
Aching on a statinAfter a statin is started; CK high
Hypothyroid myopathy
Fatigue, weight gain, bradycardia, delayed reflexesThyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) high, CK high
Glucocorticoid-induced myopathyPainless proximal weakness on long-term glucocorticoids, as for arteritisESR and CK both normal; no pain
FibromyalgiaWidespread pain with tender points, often a younger womanChronic; ESR, CRP and CK normal
4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext move
Painless proximal weakness on long-term glucocorticoids; ESR and CK normalGlucocorticoid-induced myopathy, not a flareNot more prednisone: the ESR is normal and there is no pain
Aching on a statin with a raised CKStatin myopathyStop the statin
Widespread tender points, normal ESR, CRP and CKFibromyalgiaExercise; duloxetine or another antidepressant, or an anticonvulsant
Small-joint synovitis, erosionsElderly-onset rheumatoid arthritisRheumatoid factor and anti-CCP; methotrexate

Pause point. The bait: reading "cannot get out of bed" as weakness and sending for electromyography and biopsy, or giving the high arteritis dose for polymyalgia without arteritis symptoms.

5Diagnostic criteria
Defining criteria Who – age over 50 · Pain – bilateral shoulder and hip girdle aching, morning stiffness over 60 minutes, normal strength · Labs – ESR raised, usually over 50; CRP raised; CK normal · Response – dramatic improvement on low-dose prednisone within days
6Severity
What raises the stakes
FindingMeansDo
Headache, jaw claudication, vision changeGiant cell arteritis, with a blindness riskHigh-dose glucocorticoids now; IV pulse if vision is impaired
Long-term prednisoneOsteoporosis, diabetes, hypertensionA bisphosphonate; check glucose and blood pressure
Relapse whenever the dose is loweredGlucocorticoid dependenceThe lowest dose that controls symptoms Steroid-sparingIn practice: methotrexate is an option when the glucocorticoid cannot be tapered without a relapse, though the data are limited; nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs alone are rarely enough.
7Treatment
1

Startpolymyalgia without arteritis symptoms

Low-dose prednisone, about 15 mg daily
2

Tapersymptoms subside

Taper to the lowest effective dose, by symptoms rather than the ESR
3

Raiseno response after a week

Not a higher dose: reconsider the diagnosis
4

Switchheadache, jaw claudication or vision change

High-dose glucocorticoids, about 40 to 60 mg of prednisone; IV pulse if vision is impaired; biopsy after
8Follow-up
Hours to days relief on low-dose prednisone
Weeks to months taper as symptoms subside
About 2 years some patients stop; others need small doses for years
Any time arteritis can appear, even after apparent cure
Follow-up decisions
WhenDo
Every visit, during and after treatmentAsk about headache, pain on chewing and vision change: report them at once
While taperingFollow symptoms and CRP rather than the ESR
On long-term prednisoneA bisphosphonate; watch for diabetes and hypertension
Practice
  1. 72 yo F, bilateral shoulder and hip girdle aching, morning stiffness 90 min, ESR 62, strength 5/5 → Polymyalgia rheumatica → prednisone 15 mg daily
  2. 72 yo F with known PMR, new jaw claudication and temporal tenderness → Giant cell arteritis → high-dose prednisone immediately, biopsy after
  3. 68 yo M, progressive proximal weakness, CK 4,000, normal ESR → Polymyositis → EMG and muscle biopsy
  4. 70 yo F on atorvastatin, proximal aching, CK 900 → Statin myopathy → stop the statin and recheck CK
  5. 66 yo F, proximal aching, ESR 12, TSH 14 → Hypothyroid myopathy → levothyroxine
  6. 74 yo F with presumed PMR, no response after a week of prednisone 15 mg → Reconsider the diagnosis – PMR responds within days
  7. 63 yo F, widespread pain, non-restorative sleep, normal ESR and CK → Fibromyalgia
Pearls PMR (polymyalgia rheumatica) = pain with normal CK (creatine kinase); polymyositis = weakness with high CK · PMR responds to low-dose steroids, GCA (giant cell arteritis) needs high dose · every PMR diagnosis gets a GCA symptom screen, and ~50% of GCA patients have PMR · NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) fail in PMR; they are a close but inadequate therapy.
